title: Always tired after meals? It might not be willpower.
What insulin actually does
body: Insulin is a hormone made by your pancreas that works like a key to let blood sugar (glucose) pass from your bloodstream into your muscles, liver, and fat cells for energy. Any unused glucose is stored for later.

title: What happens when you are insulin resistant?
body:
• Your cells respond less to the insulin "key"
• Your pancreas works overtime to pump out extra insulin to force glucose into your cells
• Your fasting blood sugar can look normal for years even while your insulin levels are elevated behind the scenes
• Over time, when the insulin-producing cells in your pancreas wear out, they cannot make enough insulin
• Your blood sugar rises, setting the stage for *prediabetes* and *type 2 diabetes*

title: How it affects your health
body:
Besides *prediabetes* and *type 2 diabetes*, insulin resistance contributes to:
• Increased *Cardiovascular Disease* risks as insulin resistance is often tied to metabolic syndromes such as high blood pressure, high triglycerides, unhealthy cholesterol levels, and a large waistline
• *Fatty Liver Disease* (MASLD)
• *Polycystic Ovary Syndrome* (PCOS)
• *Cognitive Decline* as insulin resistance impairs brain glucose metabolism, disrupting brain cell energy production and usage, which in turn accelerates neurodegeneration

title: Signs and symptoms of insulin resistance
body:
• Often no clear signs for years
• Dark, velvety skin patches or skin tags, usually around the neck or underarms
• Frequent cravings for sugary/ starchy foods
• Fatigue after meals
• Weight gain or trouble losing weight, particularly around the belly

title: The surprising part about insulin resistance
body:
•  Often silently develops 10 to 20 years or more before high blood sugar test shows up
• You can still have it even at a normal weight due to hidden visceral fat (fat around your organs) or a low personal fat threshold where your fat tissue stops expanding safely

title: How to reverse insulin resistance
body:
• Reduce simple sugars, refined carbohydrates, sugary beverages, and ultra-processed foods
• Focus on whole, unprocessed foods like non-starchy vegetables, lean proteins, fish, and healthy fats (such as avocados and nuts)
• Aim for 150 minutes of aerobic exercise with resistance training 2 to 3 times a week to build muscle mass (a major sink for clearing glucose from the blood)
• Take 10- to 15-minute walk shortly after meals to blunt blood sugar spikes
• Reduce 5% to 10% weight can significantly decrease liver and visceral fat, which helps to normalize insulin signalling

title: A normal check-up may not tell the whole story
body:
Just because your blood sugar is normal doesn't mean you are metabolically healthy.
